hop3_docs: Loosely associated statements | A loosely associated statement is a type of simple non-inferential passage wherein statements about a general subject are juxtaposed but make no inferential claim.  As a rhetorical device, loosely associated statements may be intended by the speaker to infer a claim or conclusion, but because they lack a coherent logical structure any such interpretation is subjective as loosely associated statements prove nothing and attempt no obvious conclusion.  Loosely associated statements can be said to serve no obvious purpose, such as illustration or explanation.

Simple non-inferential passage | A simple non-inferential passage is a type of nonargument characterized by the lack of a claim that anything is being proved.  Simple non-inferential passages include warnings, pieces of advice, statements of belief or opinion, loosely associated statements, and reports.  Simple non-inferential passages are nonarguments because while the statements involved may be premises, conclusions or both, the statements do not serve to infer a conclusion or support one another.  This is distinct from a logical fallacy, which indicates an error in reasoning.

Upon his return to the United States in 1881, Babcock took up the role of an agricultural chemist at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva, New York, where his first assignment was to determine the proper feed ratios of carbohydrate, fat, and protein using chemical analysis of cow excrement.
